A graphic designer is animating a circle in such a way that the area of the circle is decreasing at a rate of $12\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$ Calculate the rate at which the circumference of the circle is decreasing at the moment when the radius is  $3\,\text{cm}.$
question.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=3,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-12\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=3\,\text{cm},$ $C=2\pi (3)=6\pi \text{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-12\pi $ and $C=6\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-12\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{6\pi }{2\pi } \\ -12\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3 \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{12\pi }{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $4\pi \text{ cm/s}.$
